newsitem.title: SIERRA LEONE: Sierra Leone central bank works to reopen banks.
newsitem.headline: Sierra Leone central bank works to reopen banks.

text.p: The caretaker governor of Sierra Leone's central bank said he had persuaded its military rulers to provide protection for banks and he hoped the country's banking system would be functioning again shortly.

"Over the past few days, we have been holding meetings with the commercial banks so as to get them to reopen, but they have shown concern about the security of the banks and the nation," Christian Kargbo told Reuters in an interview.
"I have cleared this with the head of state, and he has assured me that maximum security will be provided for the banks and also for the man in the street," he added on Wednesday.
He said he would meet with commercial banks again on Thursday.

The West African country's central bank opened for the first time on Wednesday since the May 25 coup that toppled elected civilian president Ahmad Tejan Kabbah. Like the Treasury next door, it was badly damaged by fire during the fighting.

Commercial banks closed their doors after the coup, and people have since, had no access to their money, which has caused considerable hardship. Government workers' salaries have not been paid because of the damage to the Treasury.

"Sierra Leoneans are suffering, and something has to be done," Kargbo said. "We have gone hungry for many weeks. We have gone unpaid. We can't cash our cheques. Some people want to go away but they can't even pay their fares."
He said officials were working hard to get salaries paid.

"Even though the Treasury was destroyed by fire during the takeover, the accountant general is working on a plan to get public workers paid. Most of the computers holding the names of workers and also past salary vouchers were burnt in the fire," he said.

Kargbo, who was development and economic planning minister in the previous military government that handed over power to Kabbah last year, confirmed that the World Bank and International Monetary Fund had cut off aid to Sierra Leone after the coup.
Coup leader Johnny Paul Koroma was sworn in as head of state on Tuesday.
Kargbo said the military authorities had asked him to take over as governor of the bank.

"I turned the offer down but offered to advise them. Something has to go on in the interim while they are pursuing negotiations with the RUF (the rebel Revolutionary United Front) and the international community," he said.
The rebels, who took up arms in 1991, rallied to the coup and their heavily armed fighters flooded into the capital Freetown. They are now a key part of any negotiated settlement.
Kargbo appealed to donors not to impose sanctions on Sierra Leone.

"What they should do is come and examine the problems. Most of us do not favour military rule. Let the international community come and see what could be done to resolve our problems, so that we do not die, of hunger or otherwise."
